abstract: Myofibroblast-like cancer-associated fibroblasts (myCAFs) drive the stiff, tumor-promoting microenvironment, yet their mechanical phenotype in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains undefined. myCAFs from major NSCLC subtypes (lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC)) were examined combining atomic force microscopy and traction force microscopy with molecular and signaling analyses. LUAD-myCAFs displayed canonical myofibroblast features, including elevated stiffness, traction forces, ROCK-MYPT1 signaling, and -SMA-rich stress fibers. Unexpectedly, LUSC-myCAFs amplified these nanomechanical features despite reduced ROCK-MYPT1 signaling and comparable -SMA levels. Instead, they exhibited a smooth muscle cell (SMC)-like contractile program characterized by enhanced SM-MHC(MYH11) expression colocalized with -SMA, ERK1/2-RLC hyperactivation, and DNA methylation reprogramming including SMC-contractility regulators. LUSC-myCAF hypercontractility was linked with reduced proliferative capacity and smaller intratumoral vessel lumens, consistent with the low CAF density and enhanced hypoxia patterns reported in LUSC. SMC markers were enriched and associated with adverse outcomes selectively in LUSC, highlighting the relevance of SMC-like myCAFs in LUSC progression. These findings unveil subtype-specific myCAF programs in NSCLC, and identify -SMA/SM-MHC(MYH11) myCAFs as key determinants of tumor mechanics, providing a rationale for the survival benefits of antihypertensive drugs targeting SMC hypercontractility. Moreover, they demonstrate that nanomechanical phenotyping can uncover translationally relevant myCAF phenotypes invisible to molecular profiling.

summary: Wet-lab AFM and traction microscopy show LUSC myofibroblasts adopt SMC-like hypercontractility, unlike LUAD, with links to adverse outcomes.
title: Nanomechanical phenotyping uncovers a non-canonical smooth muscle-like hypercontractility program in lung squamous cell carcinoma myofibroblasts
